I am 50 years old and have farmed in Quzhou County my whole life. I never went to school, but I know this land the way my mother and father knew it. Every year, we plant winter wheat in the autumn and follow it with summer corn after the harvest in June. That is the way of the North China Plain, and it is what I will do again this year. I have five mu of good flat land. The wheat is already in the ground from last October — I used improved wheat seeds from the township supply store because they are reliable and not as costly as the newest hybrids. Now that spring has come, I will top-dress the wheat with urea when it greens up, irrigate three or four times depending on the rain, and spray for aphids and rust if they appear. I till with the plough before wheat sowing because the soil gets hard over summer. After I cut the wheat in early June, I will rotary-till the stubble quickly and plant hybrid corn seed — corn must be hybrid or the yield is too poor to bother with. The corn will need nitrogen at the big trumpet stage, and I will irrigate two or three times, especially if July turns dry. I use pesticides only when I see damage; twice for each crop is usually enough. I do not trust no-tillage — the weeds grow too fast and the ground becomes too hard for my small tractor. I expect about 450 kg per mu for the wheat and about 550 kg per mu for the corn if the weather is fair and the market price is decent.
